verdicts.why: In 'of no account' or 'of some account' the word names worth or importance plainly; any dismissal comes from the quantifier, not from the noun.
A report or telling of events; 'a good account' or 'different accounts' are judged by their modifiers, and the noun itself takes no side.
The 'turn to account' sense names the use or advantage got from something without approving or scorning it.
Treatment received, as in 'a fair deal' or 'a raw deal'; the adjective carries any judgement and the noun is a neutral slot for it.
Distributing cards at a table is a plain procedural act with no attitude attached.
The hand a player holds is a descriptive card-game term, judging nothing.
An act of apportioning or sharing out, named without approval or contempt.
A softwood plank is a concrete material object; there is nothing here to judge.
A trade name for pine or fir timber, purely descriptive.
Coming into view, as in 'her appearance created surprise', is an event stated flatly with no attitude toward the person who appears.
A mental picture of how someone or something looks is neutral description; the pretence sense ('the appearance of what is right') is a different synset and not the one printed here.
Formal attendance in court is a legal procedural term carrying no judgement of the party.
To decide or fix upon a course is stated without praise or blame for the decider; 'determined to hate' gets its edge from 'hate'.
Fixing something conclusively or by authority describes the act; even Lady Catherine 'determining' the weather is ironic through the situation, not the verb.
To find out with certainty, as in 'she could scarcely determine', is a plain verb of ascertaining.
Fixing the scope or boundaries of something is a technical, attitude-free sense.
Settling a matter or coming to terms is described neutrally, with no view of the parties.
A source of anxiety is an unpleasant referent named in the plain word; 'headache' or 'vexation' would be the loaded neighbours, and 'concern' is the measured one.
A business enterprise, a neutral commercial term.
A broadcast programme of current events is named descriptively; 'good' or 'dreadful' news is judged by its adjective.
Newsworthiness as a quality is stated without approving or scorning what has it.
The disposal or getting rid of something is a formal, register-marked term but carries no attitude toward the thing disposed of.
A sense of the comic is a trait people value, but the word names the trait rather than praising its holder; 'good-humour' and 'ill-humour' are judged by their prefixes.
One of the four medieval bodily fluids is a historical-medical term with no attitude.
The liquid parts of the body, an anatomical term judging nothing.
